opus-5.5.text:
Efficiency is one of those words that gets treated as the obvious virtue, but I think it can be misleading when we talk about representation, especially in evolution.

When people think about optimization, they think about getting to a target as cheaply as possible: fewer parameters, fewer steps, less compute. That's a fine goal if you know where you're going. But evolution doesn't know where it's going. There's no objective out there saying "make a human" or "make a flower." So the question of what makes a representation good is different in that setting. It's less about efficiently encoding the current solution and more about whether the representation sets you up for what comes next.

What I find interesting is that evolution does produce representations that look remarkably efficient, but in a deeper sense than parameter count. Think about how a genome encodes a body. It isn't storing a blueprint of every cell. It uses regularities like symmetry, repetition, and repetition with variation. You get two arms, and they're roughly mirror images; fingers that share a common theme. That's a kind of compression, but it's compression that respects the underlying structure of the thing being built. It's a well-organized, factored description of the world, not just a small one.

Representations like that are efficient in a way that also makes them evolvable. If the genome has captured "symmetry" as a concept, then a single mutation can change both sides of the body coherently. You're not stuck making a thousand coordinated changes by luck. So the efficiency and the evolvability are almost the same thing viewed from different angles. A representation that has carved the world at its joints is both compact and a good springboard for further discovery.

Contrast that with what we often see from conventional gradient-based training. You can get a network that performs very well on the objective, maybe even with a reasonable number of parameters, but when you look inside, the representation can be what I'd call fractured or entangled. It works, but not for the "right" reasons. It's patched together. On the surface it looks like the same performance, but underneath it's a very different kind of thing, and that difference matters enormously when you ask the system to adapt, generalize, or be creative.

So my view is that efficiency shapes evolutionary representations not because evolution is directly pressured to be efficient in the narrow sense. It's because of the open-ended, accumulative way evolution builds things. You build on stepping stones, you lay down regularities early, and later innovations reuse and elaborate on them. Over a long history, that process tends to favor representations that are well organized, because those are the ones that keep opening new doors. The elegance is a byproduct of the search process, not something targeted directly.

That's an important lesson for AI. If we only measure success by whether we hit the objective efficiently, we might be blind to the quality of the representation underneath. Two systems can score the same on a benchmark and be completely different in their potential for future innovation. The path you take to a solution leaves its fingerprints on how that solution is represented, and in the long run that might be the thing that matters most.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because efficiency is one of those things that sounds like a boring engineering constraint but actually turns out to be a deep driver of what representations look like. The way I'd put it is that evolution doesn't have the luxury of being wasteful. There's a finite genome, there's finite energy, there's finite developmental time, and so there's enormous pressure to find encodings that get a lot of structure out of very little information. The human genome is, what, on the order of tens of thousands of genes, and yet it encodes a brain with on the order of a hundred trillion connections. So clearly it's not specifying each connection individually. It's found something compressed.

And what's interesting is that compression isn't just a trick to fit things into a small space. It fundamentally changes the character of the representation. When you have to reuse information, you end up with things like symmetry, repetition with variation, regularity. You get a body with two arms that are almost the same but mirrored, or a cortex that's basically a repeated column structure. Those are signatures of an efficient encoding. They're what you'd expect if the genome is more like a program that unfolds than a blueprint that lists every part.

So in my own work, this is what pushed me toward indirect encodings, things like CPPNs and HyperNEAT, where instead of evolving every weight in a network directly, you evolve a compact generative description and the structure emerges from it. And the thing I found really striking is that when you do that, the representations you get aren't just smaller, they're more evolvable. A single mutation can change something meaningful about the whole structure in a coordinated way, rather than just perturbing one weight somewhere. So efficiency and evolvability turn out to be tightly coupled. The pressure to be compact is also a pressure to be organized, and organized representations are the ones you can actually build on.

I'd also say there's a flip side, which is that efficiency in evolution is not the same as what an engineer would call optimality. Evolution is not trying to minimize some global objective. It's just that encodings that are wasteful tend to lose over time, and encodings that capture regularities tend to persist and get elaborated. So you end up with this kind of accumulated, layered elegance that nobody designed, and I think that's actually one of the most important lessons for us in machine learning. We tend to just throw more parameters at problems, and it works to a degree, but biology is telling us there's a very different route where the representation itself does a lot of the work because it had to.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish efficiency as an outcome from efficiency as the driving force. Evolution can produce representations that are very efficient, but that doesn’t mean it’s explicitly searching for the most compact encoding or the fastest way to learn.

Think about the relationship between a genome and the organism that develops from it. The genome isn’t simply a list of every component and where it goes. Development allows information to be reused: a rule can apply in many places, producing repetition and regularity without separately specifying every detail. That’s a kind of efficiency, but it also changes what evolution can discover. A small change to a developmental rule can produce a coordinated change across the organism.

So the representation is doing more than saving space. It shapes the possibilities for variation. Two representations could describe the same organism, yet mutations in those representations could lead to very different neighborhoods of possible organisms.

That’s why I’d be cautious about treating efficiency as the whole explanation. You also want to ask: what kinds of novelty does this representation make accessible? A representation that’s economical for what exists now isn’t necessarily one that makes it easy to discover something fundamentally different.

sol-6.1.text:
I think efficiency is one of the pressures that shapes a representation, but we have to be careful about what we mean by efficient. Efficient at describing something? Efficient at producing it? Or efficient at discovering something new? Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

Take a genome. It doesn’t specify every detail of an organism independently. Development reuses information, so a relatively compact description can generate an enormously complex structure. In evolutionary computation, that motivates indirect encodings: instead of encoding every connection in a neural network separately, you encode a process that generates the connections. Then you can get repetition, symmetry, and other regularities without discovering every instance independently.

But the interesting consequence isn’t just compression. It changes what evolution can discover. A mutation to a shared developmental rule might change a whole collection of related structures together. That can make some kinds of adaptation much more accessible. Of course, it also introduces biases—some structures become easier to represent than others.

So I wouldn’t say the goal is simply to find the most efficient representation. You want a representation whose biases make useful variation possible. A very compact encoding that can’t produce interesting changes isn’t going to get you very far. The deeper issue is evolvability: how does the representation turn small genetic changes into opportunities for meaningful innovation?
